The False Positive Rate will be determined based on the Specificity of the test and the Prevalence of the disease that is being tested for. Typically, a test manufacturer would supply the Sensitivity and Specificity parameters with the test. Determining these parameters requires testing against a known population where the people who have the disease are already determined using an alternative test. To my knowelege, this has not been done for the COVID tests. There is a lot of content online stating that these tests are "Highly Specific", but, without the actual test being run, that is just speculation. Are they specific when the sample also contains other corona virus strains (common cold, etc)?

So far, the nearest I've found to someone giving an actual number on specificity is:

Researchers at the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics, a nonprofit research center in Geneva, Switzerland tested five COVID-19 RT-PCR tests and found that all five achieved 100 percent sensitivity on positive samples, and at least 96 percent specificity on negative samples in a laboratory setting.

https://www.popsci.com/story/science/covid-test-inaccuracies/

That is in a laboratory setting, so not likely to be higher than that in practice.

The problem is that the prevalence of the virus is very low. Here in Australia, the prevalence is about 0.3% (about 3 out of every 1000 people tested will test positive). So, even if your test is very specific (say 98%), and is highly sensitive (say 100%). Then the PPV (Positive Predictive Value) of such a test would be around 13%. So, basically, when testing the general population in a low prevalence scenario, a positive test result would indicate that you might have the disease. Re-testing would be advised to confirm.

As the prevalence rate of the disease increases, the PPV of a test with the same sensitivity and specificity will increase quite quickly though. So, when testing in an isolation ward (with a prevalence of say 50%), the PPV of the same test would be 98%

Some reasonably in depth reading on this sort of stuff (and the source of my PPV equation) here: https://www.medcalc.org/manual/roc-curves.php
